narrative:
The model determined that you have a 35% chance of being a bad credit risk. While this is not an extremely high probability, it was enough for the bank to deny your loan application.

Your denial was driven by three key factors that mattered most to the model. First, your credit history of having critical or other existing credits pushed the decision toward denial. Although this history is fairly common among applicants (33% of approved customers share a similar background), the model viewed it as a warning sign that increased your risk. Second, the relatively short 11-month duration you requested for the loan worked in your favor and pulled the prediction back toward approval. Most approved applicants actually request longer terms, averaging 19 months, so your shorter request was seen positively. Third, the status of your checking account, which shows between 0 and 200 DM, worked against you. This is not uncommon (18% of approved applicants are in the same range), but the model interpreted it as contributing to higher risk compared with those who have no checking account or larger balances.

In summary, your credit history and checking account status outweighed the positive effect of your shorter loan duration, tipping the balance against approval.

You should focus on improving your credit history by paying down existing debts on time. Once your record shows consistent, on-time payments, consider reapplying. This is the clearest step that would most likely change future model decisions in your favor. (218 words)
